name: The Pilate Stone
found: 1961 · reused as a stair step in the Roman theater at Caesarea Maritima
inscription: To the Divine Augusti [this] Tiberieum … Pontius Pilate … prefect of Judaea … has dedicated [this].
inscriptionNote: Latin, four damaged lines (AE 1963 no. 104). “Pilatus” and “prefect of Judaea” are the securely legible core; the first and last lines are scholarly restorations, and the restorations are debated.
attests: the only contemporary inscription naming Pontius Pilate
his exact title — prefect of Judaea
location: Israel Museum, Jerusalem (replicas at Caesarea and Milan)
note: An Italian expedition led by Antonio Frova found the block where fourth-century builders had recycled it as a step. It is the earliest physical witness to the governor who, in Tacitus and the gospels alike, sentenced Jesus — and it quietly corrects Tacitus, who called Pilate “procurator”: the stone says prefect.
limits: The inscription does not mention Jesus or any trial. Its damaged first and last lines are reconstructed, although Pilate’s name and title are secure.

name: The Caiaphas Ossuary
found: 1990 · a burial cave broken open during park construction in the Peace Forest, south Jerusalem
inscription: Yehosef bar Qayafa — “Joseph, son of Caiaphas”
inscriptionNote: Aramaic, scratched twice on the box. Josephus gives the high priest’s full name as “Joseph, who was called Caiaphas.”
attests: the Caiaphas family name in 1st-century Jerusalem, as the gospels and Josephus give it
an unusually ornate ossuary holding, among others, a man of about sixty
if the identification holds — the burial box of the high priest at Jesus’ hearing
note: The identification is probable, not proven, and scholars have said so plainly: the spelling is not a perfect match for “Caiaphas,” the inscription carries no title, and the tomb is modest for a high-priestly family. Supporters answer with the ornate box and the match of name and age. This page keeps it at “probable.”
limits: The box carries no priestly title and cannot be proven to belong to the Gospel high priest. It establishes the name and burial setting more securely than the individual identity.

name: The heel bone of Yehohanan
found: 1968 · a tomb opened by construction work at Giv’at ha-Mivtar, north-east Jerusalem
inscriptionNote: Aramaic, on his ossuary; the second name’s meaning is uncertain.
attests: skeletal evidence of Roman crucifixion — an iron nail through the heel
crucified victims in Judea could receive proper Jewish burial
crucifixion practiced in Jerusalem in Jesus’ own century
location: Bones reburied per Jewish custom; the ossuary and a replica of the nailed heel are shown in the Israel Museum, Jerusalem
note: An 11.5 cm nail had bent against a knot in the olive wood and could not be pulled out, so it was buried with him. The corrected analysis (Zias & Sekeles, 1985) reads one heel nailed and the arms likely tied. For half a century this was the only skeletal evidence of crucifixion found anywhere — and it answers, in bone, the claim that crucified men were never given burial.
limits: Yehohanan is a different victim. His remains demonstrate a practice and the possibility of burial, not the exact nailing method or burial history of Jesus.

name: The Galilee Boat
found: 1986 · the exposed lakebed near Kibbutz Ginosar, during a drought, by two fishermen brothers
attests: the kind of fishing boat the gospels presuppose
the patched, modest economy of Galilean fishermen
note: Cedar planking on oak frames with ten different woods worked in — repaired again and again, finally stripped and scuttled. Nothing connects this boat to Jesus or any disciple, and this page makes no such claim. What it fixes is the setting: the working world of Peter, Andrew, James, and John, at exactly their time.
limits: Nothing connects this vessel to Jesus or any disciple. It reconstructs the working environment described by the Gospels, not a specific episode.

name: Capernaum — the house under the octagon
found: excavated from 1968 · the insula sacra at Capernaum (Corbo and Loffreda)
artifactDate: 1st-century-BC house, singled out by the mid-1st century AD
inscription: In Capernaum the house of the prince of the apostles has been made into a church, with its original walls still standing.
inscriptionNote: Not an inscription — the pilgrim Egeria’s travel diary, c. AD 380, describing what she found there.
attests: a plain 1st-century house set apart and venerated from very early
an unbroken chain on one spot: house → house-church → 5th-century octagonal shrine
a real 1st-century town the gospels call “his own city”
location: Beneath the modern memorial church (glass floor), Franciscan custody, Capernaum
note: That the house was Peter’s rests on the chain of veneration and on Egeria — not on a deed, and the excavators’ readings of the graffiti are contested. The white limestone synagogue beside it is 4th–5th century, but it stands on basalt foundations that may belong to the synagogue of Mark 1:21. Both attributions are argued; neither is proven.
limits: The site preserves early veneration, but no deed identifies Peter and the graffiti readings are contested. It cannot prove Jesus stayed in this particular house.

name: The Magdala synagogue and its stone
found: 2009 · a salvage dig before hotel construction at Migdal, on the Sea of Galilee
attests: a Galilean synagogue standing during Jesus’ teaching years
one of the earliest carved images of the Temple menorah
Galilee’s live connection to the Jerusalem Temple
location: In situ at the Magdala archaeological park
note: The gospels say Jesus taught “in their synagogues throughout all Galilee,” and for a long time no first-century Galilean synagogue was known — some doubted the texts on exactly this point. Magdala, Mary Magdalene’s hometown, produced one in 2009 and a second in 2021. At the first one’s center lay a carved stone bearing a seven-branched menorah, plausibly cut by someone who had seen the real one. What the stone’s full imagery means is still argued.
limits: The synagogue does not prove that Jesus taught in this building, and the carved stone’s full meaning remains debated. It establishes the kind of Galilean setting.
